The present claim petition is based on DAR filed by IO for claiming compensation on account of the injuries sustained by petitioner Sh. Pawan Kumar Chauhan in the accident which happened on 07/10/2019.

2. Briefly stated, the facts of the claim petition are that on 07.10.2019 at about 3:30 p.m., petitioner Pawan Kumar @ Pawan Chauhan was standing near to his vehicle, which was parked at correct side Pawan Kumar vs Ajeet Kumar on 10 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76139697/
1 of the road at Service Road near Taj Apartment, Ghazipur Village.
He was supervising the loading and unloading of the goods in his company's vehicle.

Suddenly, a TATA ACE (chhota Hathi) bearing Registration No.DL-1LY-2807, being driven by Respondent No.1 at a very high speed, rashly and recklessly in a zig zag manner without following the traffic rules, came from TARANG Banquet side and hit him with great force.
As a result, he fall down on road and sustained multiple grievous injuries.
He was immediately admitted to MAX Hospital, Patparganj in pathetic condition, where his MLC was prepared and he was treated by the doctors.
Case Crime bearing no.0159/19 u/s 279/338 IPC at PS- Patparganj Industrial Area, Delhi. was registered in connection with the accident.
3. In response to the notice of petition, R3/Insurer filed its replies/ written statements.
3(i). R1 & R2 have not filed their replies despite opportunities granted.

Respondent No.3 / Tata AIG GIC has filed its written statement and has taken the plea that as per the report of Investigation Officr, the driver supplied a fake driving licence, for which he has been challaned.
It is further submitted that the vehicle was being driven by the accused driver without valid and effective licence.
Other general defences have been taken by R3/Insurer.

4. On the basis of the pleadings of the parties, following issues were framed on 01.09.2022:-
(i) Whether the petitioner Mr. Pawan Kumar suffered grievous injuries in a motor vehicular accident which happened on 07.10.2019 at about 03:30 pm at Ghazipur,
Delhi, within jurisdiction of PS PIA, due to rash and negligent driving of Goods Carrier (open body) bearing Registration No. DL-1LY-2807 being driven by Respondent No.1 / Ajeet Kumar?

(OPP) 
(ii) Whether there was breach of terms and conditions of the insurance policy, as the driver of the offending vehicle was not holding valid and effective driving licence at the time of accident?
If yes, its effect?
(OPR3)
(iii) Whether the petitioner is entitled to compensation on account of said injuries and if yes, to what extent and from whom?

(OPP) 
(iv) Relief.

8. The issues are decided as follows:-
ISSUE NO. 1:-
9.
In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and in fact is the preponderance of probabilities which is applied in civil cases.
It is also the law that the tribunal is not bound by the technical rules of evidence.
Further, in holding any inquiry under section 168, The Claims Tribunal may follow such summary procedure as it thinks fit.
10. Now in this case, the petitioner Pawan Kumar is injured and witness of the accident.
(As per DAR & medical documents, name of injured is 'Pawan Kumar'.
However, in the copy of aadhar card & PAN card, his name is mentioned as 'Pawan Chauhan' S/o Ram pal Singh Chauhan).

In order to establish his claim, he stated on oath that on 07.10.2019 at about 3:30 p.m., petitioner Pawan Chauhan was standing near to his vehicle, which was parked at correct side of the road at Service Road near Taj Apartment, Ghazipur Village.
He was supervising the loading and unloading of the goods in his company's vehicle.

Suddenly, a TATA ACT (chhota Hathi) bearing Registration No.
DL-1LY-2807 being driven by Respondent No.1 at a very high speed, rashly and recklessly in a zig zag manner without following the traffic rules came from TARANG Banquet side and hit him with great force.
As a result, he fell down on road and sustained multiple grievous injuries.
He was immediately admitted to MAX Hospital, Patparganj in pathetic condition, where his MLC was prepared and he was treated by the doctors.
Case Crime bearing no.0159/19 u/s 279/338 IPC at PS- Patparganj Industrial Area, Delhi. was registered in connection with the accident.
FIR was registered on the same day.
11. After investigation, police filed the charge-sheet against respondent no. 1/ the driver of the offending vehicle.
Filing of charge-sheet against the driver of offending vehicle prima-facie points to his culpability.

In New India Assurance Company Ltd vs Pazhaniammal (2011) (2) KLT 648, the Hon'ble High Court of Kerala has held that as a general rule, it can be accepted that production of charge-sheet is prima facie sufficient evidence of negligence for the purpose of claim under section 166 MV Act.

sentences.text: If any party does not accept such charge-sheet, the burden must be on such party to adduce evidence.

If the Tribunal feels that charge-sheet is collusive, it can record that charge-sheet cannot be accepted and call upon the parties at any stage to adduce oral evidence of accident and alleged negligence.
In such cases, issue of negligence must be decided on other evidence ignoring the charge-sheet.
No evidence was led by any of the respondents in their defence and R1 did not enter into witness box to assail the claim of the petitioner.
13. Respondent Nos.1 and 2 (the driver and owner of the offending vehicle), did not lead any evidence to prove anything contrary to the claim of the petitioner.

In the case of Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Cmpany Ltd vs Smt. Kamlesh and Others2009 (3) AD Delhi 310 it was held that an adverse inference can be drawn when the driver of the offending vehicle does not enter into the witness box.

A suggestion was given to the petitioner that he was standing in middle of the road,
which was denied by him.
MLC of petitioner, which is part of charge-sheet attached with DAR reflects that petitioner sustained grievous injuries.

14. In view of above, on the basis of preponderance of probabilities of evidence and for filing of charge-sheet, it is proved that the petitioner Pawan Kumar received grievous injuries due to rash and negligent act of respondent no.1/Ajeet Kumar, the driver of the offending vehicle.

Accordingly,
this issue is decided in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents.

15. The next question to be decided by the Tribunal whether there is breach of terms and conditions of the insurance policy by the insured so as to absolve the insurance company from the duty to compensate the injured.

In this regard, respondent No.3 / insurer examined R3W1 Ms. Poornima Malhotra, Legal associate with insurance company, who deposed that despite service of notice to the registered owner of the offending vehicle, he did not produce the driving licence of the respondent No.1 and it shows that he willingly entrusted his vehicle to R-1, who was not having a valid driving licence.
In the case in hand, insurance company has pleaded that R-1 / driver did not have a valid driving licence at the time of accident.
Ld. Counsel for R-3 submitted that as per the charge-sheet filed by the IO, R-1 had supplied a fake driving licence and he was booked for offences u/s 420/468/471 IPC in the charge-sheet.

R-3 sent notice to R-2 Mr. Satbir Singh for producing the valid driving licence of R-1 but R-2 failed to produce the driving licence of R-1 which clearly shows the terms and conditions of insurance policy were breached by R-2, by entrusting his vehicle to R-1.
This witness was not cross-examined by any of the respondents No.1 and 2.
She was cross-examined by Ld. Counsel for the petitioner but nothing material could come out during her cross-examination.
R-1 has been charge-sheeted under relevant provisions of law for having a fake licence.
R-1 did not produce any other licence during entire investigation or even before the Tribunal.
Now the question is whether there was any breach of insurance policy by R-2 / registered owner by virtue of the fact that R-1 had a fake driving licence.

R-3 has not led any evidence to show that R-2 had knowledge Pawan Kumar vs Ajeet Kumar on 10 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76139697/
4 that the driving licence produced by R-1 was fake or that he allowed R-1 to drive his vehicle, despite such knowledge.
Mere non filing of written statement or reply to the notice of R-3 by R-2 does not mean an admission on the part of the R-2 in this regard.

R-3 failed to lead any independent evidence to suggest that R-3 had any duty to verify the driving licence or had verified the driving licence and found it to be fake or that he had learnt from anyone that DL was fake but despite it, he allowed R-1 to drive his vehicle.
Further, it is not the plea taken by R-3 that driving licence on the very face of it looked fake.
There is nothing brought on record by R-3 to suggest that R-2 had any role to play in the preparation of fake driving licence or that he was informed by anyone that the DL of R-1 was fake.

16. In the case titled as IFFCO Tokio General Insurance Co Ltd Vs Geeta Devi and Others decided on 13.10.2023, the Division Bench of Apex Court, while observing that no evidence has been placed on record whereby inference can be drawn that the vehicle owner ought to have gotten verified driver's driving licence, held that :-
"15.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: As already pointed out Supra , once a seemingly valid driving licence is produced by a person employed to drive a vehicle, unless such licence is demonstrably fake on the face of it, warranting any sensible employer to make inquiries as to its genuineness, or when the period of the licence has already expired, or there is some other reason to entertain a genuine doubt as to its validity, the burden is upon the insurance company to prove that there was a failure on the part of the vehicle owner in carrying out due diligence apropos such driving licence before employing that person to drive the vehicle," presently no evidence has been placed on record wherebyan inference could be drawn that the deceased vehicle owner ought to have gotten verified Ujay Pal's driving licence.
Therefore, it was for the petitioner - insurance company to prove willful breach on the part of the said vehicle owner.

As no such exercise was undetaken, the petitioner - insurance company would have no right to recover the compensation amount from the present owners of the vehicle.."
17.
In the case of Ram Chandra Singh Vs Rajaram and others' (2018) wherein it was held by Hon'ble Supreme Court the mere fact that the driver's licence was fake, per se, would not absolve the insurer.

Hence, this issue is decided against respondent No.3 / insurer and it is held that R-2 / insured /
registered owner of the offending vehicle did not breach the terms and condition of the insurance policy.

ISSUE No.3:
18.
Section 168 of the Act enjoins the Claims Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and reasonable.
The compensation should not be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.
19. The case of Raj Kumar vs Ajay Kumar & Another (2011) 1 SCC 343, is one of the most prominent judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court which deals with compensation in injuries cases.

entities.text: Raj Kumar vs Ajay Kumar & Another (2011) 1 SCC 343
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It was held in this case that in routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under the Pawan Kumar vs Ajeet Kumar on 10 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76139697/
5
heads-(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation, nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured ,
comprising (a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment and (iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.

Where the claimant suffers a permanent disability as a result of injuries, the assessment of compensation is also to be done under the head of loss of future earnings which would depend upon the effect and impact of such permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured.
The tribunal should not mechanically apply the percentage of permanent disability as the percentage of economic loss or loss of earning capacity.

What requires to be assessed by the tribunal is the effect of the permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured after assessing the loss of earning capacity in terms of percentage of the income.
It has to be quantified in terms of money to arrive at the future loss of earnings by applying standard multiplier method.
All injuries or permanent disabilities arising from injuries do not result in loss of earning capacity.

If there is no loss of employment or earning capacity, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of loss of future earnings, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities in consequent to his injuries.

20. Therefore, on the basis of the injuries to the petitioner, the compensation is awarded to him under the afore-said heads as follows :-
MEDICAL EXPENSES:
21.
Petitioner has placed on record his original medical bills (part of document Ex.PW1/3) to the tune of Rs.831/-.
All the bills are original and in order.
No dispute has been raised by R-3/ insurer to the medical bills/ invoices filed.
Hence, an amount of Rs. 831/- is awarded to the petitioner under this head.
Some more documents have been filed as part of Ex. PW1/3 but the same cannot be called as bills by any stretch of imagination.
No bill number and amount is specified on these piece of papers.

PAIN AND SUFFERING:
22.

According to his affidavit, after the accident, the working capacity of the petitioner was totally curtailed and he was unable to handle work on his own and his family was suffering from huge financial crisis.
It is further stated that he is suffering from permanent disability and not able to stand for long hours and unable to supervise the loading unloading job.
However, the disability certificate Ex. PW1/7 does not present such a dismal picture.
It suggests permanent disability of only 6%.
No doctor was examined to show how the permanent disability sustained by the petitioner could come in the way of performance of his work as a supervisor.

The MLC which is part of DAR and criminal case record suggests that petitioner suffered from grievous injuries and discharge summary of Max Superspeciality hospital shows that petitioner remained admitted there from 07.10.2019 to 09.10.2019.
As per discharge summary, he suffered from Bimalleolar fracture on right ankle.
The medical document on record suggest petitioner visited hospital till October 2019.

Hence,
it is clear that petitioner must have remained under considerable pain.

Therefore, I find it Pawan Kumar vs Ajeet Kumar on 10 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76139697/
6 appropriate to grant a sum of Rs.30,000/- to the petitioner under this head.
CONVEYANCE, SPECIAL DIET & ATTENDANT CHARGES 23.
Petitioner has not proved any actual expenses in relation to these heads and has not placed any material on record to substantiate the said expenses.
In the given facts and circumstances of the case, I deem it fit to grant Rs.10,000/- to petitioner for conveyance and special diet charges.
24. Petitioner has claimed attendant expenses but no evidence has been led to show that petitioner had hired any attendant during his treatment.

Considering the nature of injuries as reflected through the medical documents placed on record, there cannot be an inference that actual services of any family member were consistently required by the petitioner for any given period of time.
He sustained grievous injuries and hence it is quite possible that his family members might have rendered him some assistance.
Therefore, the petitioner is awarded a sum of Rs.10,000/- as attendant charges.
25. Thus, petitioner is granted a total compensation of Rs.20,000/- (10,000+10,000) under this head.

LOSS OF INCOME DURING TREATMENT :
26.

Petitioner has claimed that he was working as a supervisor in delivery company and earning Rs.
20,000/- per month.
According to him, at the time of accident, he was supervising the loading and unloading of goods in the company's vehicle.
During his cross-examination, he failed to disclose the registration number of vehicle on which loading and unloading was being done as claimed by him.
Petitioner deposed that he has not placed on record his salary slip or bank statement.
Petitioner has not disclosed the name of his employer, the address of his employer and no proof of income and job has been filed on record by him.
The petitioner has placed on record marksheet of his 10th class and marksheet of 11th class second term.

Hence his salary is estimated as per the minimum wages applicable to a skilled worker in Delhi at the time of accident (as petitioner is stated to be a resident of Delhi) which is Rs.17,991/- per month.

Considering the nature of injuries being grievous, the period and course of treatment and keeping in mind the nature of job of the petitioner, it is not difficult to presume that in case of fracture and injuries sustained as above-mentioned, Petitioner must have been disabled from work for about two months as this would have been the minimum time to heal.
Therefore, I award Rs.35,982/- (17991x2) as compensation under this head.

Therefore,
his loss of income for two months is calculated as Rs.35,982/-.
LOSS OF FUTURE INCOME ON ACCOUNT OF PERMANENT DISABILITY.
27. The next question that remains to be decided is the compensation with respect to the disability of the petitioner.
Under this head, it has to be seen that what could be the future loss of income on account of disability.
The disability certificate of Dr. Hedgewar Arogya Sansthan clearly shows that the petitioner is the case of 6% disability.
No doctor from disability board has been examined as an expert witness on disability certificate issued by the Disability Board.

According to the disability Pawan Kumar vs Ajeet Kumar on 10 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76139697/
7 certificate Ex.PW1/7, petitioner suffered 6% permanent disability.

sentences.text: Petitioner has failed to file on record any document in support of his job and salary and nature of work.

There is nothing brought on record to suggest that PW1 was doing a job involving long hours of standing or that due to permanent disability he was incapable to do so, other than his bald oral assertion in this regard.
A suggestion was given by Ld. counsel for R-3 that he has fully recovered and has no difficulty in doing his day-to-day work or professional engagement.
Petitioner has not examined his employer to suggest that he has any loss of income and change in the nature of job or working hours due to permanent disability suffered by him.
There is nothing brought on record by petitioner to suggest that he was unable to work after the accident.
He has not proved that due to this injury, his income has reduced.

Petitioner has not led any documentary evidence to show what work he was doing prior to accident and what work is being done by him in his work place post-accident, to arrive at any conclusion that petitioner's nature of job has changed drastically to his detriment and that it is due to accident solely.
It is not the plea of the petitioner that he has suffered from any loss of income on account of accident.
Rather, petitioner has not even led any cogent evidence to prove his occupation and income.

In case titled as Ramvir Singh Vs. Rajesh Kumar & Ors. MAC Appeal 812/11 decided on 30.11.2012 by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi, no compensation under this head was awarded, where it was found that the police official concerned had not suffered from any professional loss on account of disability.

Arising out of civil appeal No. 8918 of 2010, it was held by Hon'ble Supreme Court that :-
10.
Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.

The Tribunal has to first ascertain what activities the claim could carry on inspite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of the permanent disability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The second step is to ascertain his avocation, profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age.

The third step is to find out whether ; (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood, or (ii) whether inspite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions, but could carry on some other or lesser scale of activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood.
For example, if the left hand of the claimant is amputated, the permanent physical or disablement may be around 60%.
If the claimant was a driver of a carpenter, the actual loss of earning capacity may virtually be 100%, if he is neither able to drive or do carpentry.

On the other hand, if the claimant is clerk in government service, the loss of his left hand may not result in loss of employment and he may still be continued as a clerk as he could performed his clerical functions, in that even the loss of earnings capacity will not be 100% as in the case of a driver or carpenter nor 60% which is the actual physical disability but far less.

In fact, there may not be need to award any compensation under the head of 'Loss of future earnings', if the claimant continues in Government service, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities on the consequences of losing his hand....."

INTEREST 30.
Petitioner has pursued his case since year 2020.
Therefore, he is entitled for interest @ 7.5% per annum on the aforesaid award amount from the date of filing of the petition till realization.

LIABILITY:
31.
Now, the question arises as to which of the respondents is liable to pay the compensation amount.
As insurance company has contractual and statutory liability to indemnify the insured, the Insurance company is liable to compensate the third party.
In view of above, it is held that respondent no.3/ insurer shall be liable to pay the compensation amount to the petitioner.

RELIEF:
32.

In view of the findings on above points, I as presiding officer of this Tribunal award a total compensation of Rs.87,000 /- (Rupees eighty seven Thousand only) along with interest @ 7.5% per annum on the aforesaid award amount from the date of filing of the petition till realization in favour of petitioner against the respondent no.3/ insurer.
This award is required to be deposited with this Tribunal within 30 days.
33. With these observations, the present claim petition is disposed off.
34. File be consigned to Record Room.

12. In New India Assurance Company Ltd vs Pazhaniammal (2011) (2) KLT 648, the Hon'ble High Court of Kerala has held that as a general rule, it can be accepted that production of charge-sheet is prima facie sufficient evidence of negligence for the purpose of claim under section 166 MV Act.

If the Tribunal feels that charge-sheet is collusive, it can record that charge-sheet cannot be accepted and call upon the parties at any stage to adduce oral evidence of accident and alleged negligence.
In such cases, issue of negligence must be decided on other evidence ignoring the charge-sheet.
No evidence was led by any of the respondents in their defence and R1 did not enter into witness box to assail the claim of the petitioner.
In the case of Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Cmpany Ltd vs Smt. Kamlesh and Others2009 (3) AD Delhi 310 it was held that an adverse inference can be drawn when the driver of the offending vehicle does not enter into the witness box.
R-1 did not produce any other licence during entire investigation or even before the Tribunal.
Mere non filing of written statement or reply to the notice of R-3 by R-2 does not mean an admission on the part of the R-2 in this regard.
R-3 failed to lead any independent evidence to suggest that R-3 had any duty to verify the driving licence or had verified the driving licence and found it to be fake or that he had learnt from anyone that DL was fake but despite it, he allowed R-1 to drive his vehicle.
Further, it is not the plea taken by R-3 that driving licence on the very face of it looked fake.
There is nothing brought on record by R-3 to suggest that R-2 had any role to play in the preparation of fake driving licence or that he was informed by anyone that the DL of R-1 was fake.
19. The case of Raj Kumar vs Ajay Kumar & Another (2011) 1 SCC 343, is one of the most prominent judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court which deals with compensation in injuries cases.
Where the claimant suffers a permanent disability as a result of injuries, the assessment of compensation is also to be done under the head of loss of future earnings which would depend upon the effect and impact of such permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured.
The tribunal should not mechanically apply the percentage of permanent disability as the percentage of economic loss or loss of earning capacity.
What requires to be assessed by the tribunal is the effect of the permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured after assessing the loss of earning capacity in terms of percentage of the income.
It has to be quantified in terms of money to arrive at the future loss of earnings by applying standard multiplier method.
All injuries or permanent disabilities arising from injuries do not result in loss of earning capacity.
If there is no loss of employment or earning capacity, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of loss of future earnings, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities in consequent to his injuries.
Therefore, I find it Pawan Kumar vs Ajeet Kumar on 10 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76139697/
6 appropriate to grant a sum of Rs.30,000/- to the petitioner under this head.
Considering the nature of injuries as reflected through the medical documents placed on record, there cannot be an inference that actual services of any family member were consistently required by the petitioner for any given period of time.
He sustained grievous injuries and hence it is quite possible that his family members might have rendered him some assistance.
Petitioner has failed to file on record any document in support of his job and salary and nature of work.
There is nothing brought on record to suggest that PW1 was doing a job involving long hours of standing or that due to permanent disability he was incapable to do so, other than his bald oral assertion in this regard.
Petitioner has not led any documentary evidence to show what work he was doing prior to accident and what work is being done by him in his work place post-accident, to arrive at any conclusion that petitioner's nature of job has changed drastically to his detriment and that it is due to accident solely.
It is not the plea of the petitioner that he has suffered from any loss of income on account of accident.
Rather, petitioner has not even led any cogent evidence to prove his occupation and income.
In case titled as Ramvir Singh Vs. Rajesh Kumar & Ors. MAC Appeal 812/11 decided on 30.11.2012 by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi, no compensation under this head was awarded, where it was found that the police official concerned had not suffered from any professional loss on account of disability.
In case bearing citation Raj Kumar vs. Ajay Kumar & Ors.
Pawan Kumar vs Ajeet Kumar on 10 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76139697/
8 28.
